topic: Europe's First Total Eclipse in 27 Years
zh: 歐洲 27 年來首見日全食

a.title: The Sky Will Go Dark
text: On Wednesday, August 12, the Moon will move in front of the Sun. The sky will go dark in the middle of the day. This is called a total solar eclipse.
People in Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain will see it best. In other places, like most of Europe and Canada, people will only see part of it.
The dark time is very short. It is about two minutes.
This is very special for Europe. The last time was in 1999 — that is 27 years ago!
In Spain, the eclipse will happen in the evening. The Sun will be low in the sky, near the ground.
Millions of people will travel to see it. Scientists will study it too.
One important rule: never look at the Sun without special eclipse glasses. Normal sunglasses are not safe. The Sun can hurt your eyes very badly.

opts: How to make and use eclipse glasses
A total solar eclipse in August
Why Iceland and Spain are good for photos
Why the Moon looks so bright at night

opts: About two hours
About twenty minutes

q.why: 線索：“One important rule: never look at the Sun without special eclipse glasses.”

near the ground

q.why: low in the sky = 接近地平線。

q.q: You are in Spain to watch the eclipse near sunset. Where is the best place to stand?

A narrow street between tall city buildings
A quiet seat inside your hotel room
The bottom of a valley, away from the wind
q.why: 太陽很低，丘陵與建築可能擋住。

gt.zh: 八月十二日星期三，月亮將會移到太陽的前面。

gt.en: In Spain, the eclipse will happen in the evening.
gt.zh: 在西班牙，日食會在傍晚發生。

gt.zh: 一個重要的規則：沒有戴特殊的日食眼鏡，絕對不要直視太陽。

b.title: A Rare Eclipse Returns to Europe
text: On 12 August 2026, the Moon will pass directly between the Earth and the Sun, creating a total solar eclipse. For a short time, day will turn into night along a narrow path across the planet.

That path will begin in the Arctic, cross Greenland and the west coast of Iceland, and then travel over the Atlantic Ocean before reaching northern Spain and a small corner of Portugal. Outside this path, a partial eclipse will be visible across much of Europe, most of Canada and parts of the northern United States.

What makes the event unusual is not only where it goes, but how rare it is. According to the European Space Agency, this will be the first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999. Totality will last no more than about two and a half minutes at any single location.

In Spain, the eclipse will occur shortly before sunset, when the Sun sits very low in the sky. Photographers are excited by this, although buildings and hills could block the view for people who choose the wrong spot.

Millions of visitors are expected to travel to the path of totality, and scientists will use the moment to study the Sun's outer atmosphere. Everyone, however, is being reminded of the same safety rule: except during the brief seconds of totality, the Sun must never be viewed without certified eclipse glasses.

q.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
opts: To explain what will happen on 12 August and why it matters
To warn people that travelling to Spain for the eclipse is unsafe
To describe how eclipses have changed in Europe since 1999
To explain how scientists study the Sun's outer atmosphere

q.q: According to the text, why is this eclipse unusual?
opts: It is the longest total eclipse ever recorded in Europe
It is the first total eclipse ever seen from Iceland
It is the first visible from mainland Europe since 1999
Its dark period will last for about two hours in Spain
q.why: 原文：“According to the European Space Agency, this will be the first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999.”

q.q: Why might some people in Spain be disappointed?
opts: The path of totality will not reach Spain
Hills or buildings may block the low Sun
Totality there will last only a second or two
Too many visitors will fill the best viewing spots
q.why: 線索：“Photographers are excited by this, although buildings and hills could block the view for people who choose the wrong spot.”

q.q: In paragraph 3, “Totality” refers to ___.
opts: the whole narrow path of the eclipse
the partial eclipse seen across Europe
the total number of visitors expected
the time when the Sun is fully covered

q.q: What is the safety rule mentioned in the text?
opts: Use certified glasses, except during totality
Never look at any part of the eclipse at all
Ordinary dark sunglasses are safe to use
Look at the Sun only when it sits low at sunset
q.why: 原文：“Everyone, however, is being reminded of the same safety rule: except during the brief seconds of totality, the Sun must never be viewed without certified eclipse glasses.”

q.q: A shop sells 'eclipse glasses' with no certification label. Based on the text, what should you do?
opts: Buy them — any dark glasses protect your eyes
Avoid them — the text says to use certified glasses
Buy them, but wear them only during totality
Use your ordinary sunglasses instead of them

tr.en: Outside this path, a partial eclipse will be visible across much of Europe, most of Canada and parts of the northern United States.
tr.zh: 在這條路徑之外，歐洲大部分地區、加拿大大部分地區和美國北部的部分地區都能看到日偏食。

tr.en: What makes the event unusual is not only where it goes, but how rare it is.
tr.zh: 這次天象之所以特別，不只是因為它經過的地方，還因為它有多麼罕見。

tr.en: Millions of visitors are expected to travel to the path of totality, and scientists will use the moment to study the Sun's outer atmosphere.
tr.zh: 預計將有數百萬名遊客前往日全食帶，科學家也會利用這個時刻研究太陽的外層大氣。

c.title: Two Minutes of Darkness, Twenty-Seven Years in the Waiting
text: Total solar eclipses are, in strictly astronomical terms, unremarkable: somewhere on Earth, the Moon slides across the face of the Sun roughly every eighteen months. What makes the eclipse of 12 August 2026 significant is not the mechanics but the geography. For the first time since 1999, the Moon's darkest shadow will fall on mainland Europe.

The path is an unusual one. Rather than sweeping conventionally from west to east, this shadow arcs up over the Arctic before descending through Greenland, western Iceland and the North Atlantic, finally reaching the Iberian Peninsula as the Sun approaches the horizon. Nowhere along that track will totality exceed roughly two and a half minutes; in Spain it will arrive in the last golden minutes before sunset, low enough that a poorly chosen hillside or an inconveniently placed building could erase the spectacle entirely.

That fragility is precisely what draws people. Eclipse chasers speak of totality as categorically different from a partial eclipse — the common assumption that a 90 percent eclipse delivers 90 percent of the experience is, they insist, simply wrong. Only when the Sun's disc is fully covered does the corona, its faint outer atmosphere, become visible to the naked eye, and only then may that eye be safely uncovered.

For researchers, those seconds remain scientifically valuable, offering a rare natural view of a region of the Sun that instruments otherwise struggle to isolate. For everyone else, the appeal is harder to quantify. Millions are expected to travel; hotels along the Spanish path were reportedly booked out months in advance. What they are paying for, in the end, is a couple of minutes in which the ordinary machinery of the sky briefly, and visibly, does something else.

q.q: What is the central argument of the text?
opts: It matters for where it falls, not because eclipses are rare.
Total eclipses are extremely rare, so this one is special.
Eclipse chasers exaggerate how much a partial eclipse matters.
Its value lies mainly in what scientists can learn from it.

q.q: Why does the writer open by calling total eclipses “unremarkable”?
opts: To suggest that this particular eclipse will be boring
To set up a contrast that explains the real interest
To discourage casual visitors from travelling to watch
To criticise astronomers for overhyping eclipses

q.q: In paragraph 2, “erase the spectacle entirely” means that a hill or building could ___.
opts: make the eclipse look brighter and larger
shorten the time that totality lasts
completely block the view of the eclipse
help photographers frame the low Sun

q.q: How does the writer present the eclipse chasers' claim about 90 percent eclipses?
opts: As a proven scientific fact from the space agency
As a foolish mistake that the writer corrects
As the writer's own strongly held belief
As others' view, reported but not personally guaranteed

q.q: What does the final sentence achieve?
opts: It introduces a new topic for a later article.
It returns to brevity, giving a reflective ending.
It repeats the safety rule about certified glasses.
It lists the best places to watch from in Spain.

q.q: A friend says a 90% partial eclipse at home is 'almost the same' as totality. How should you treat this claim, based on the text?
opts: As definitely true, since 90 percent is almost all of the Sun
As an official rule published by the European Space Agency
As a claim chasers dispute — worth checking before you decide
As something the writer personally proves with evidence
q.why: 文中把該說法歸於追日者，應加以查證。

discuss: Would you travel to another country for two minutes of darkness? Why or why not?
Taiwan's last total solar eclipse was in 1941. Why do you think eclipses attract so much attention?
Should schools stop lessons so students can watch a rare natural event? Give reasons.

topic: The Biggest Stock Market Debut Ever
src: The Economist · The Washington Post · Reuters

a.title: A Rocket Company Sells Its Shares
text: On June 12, people could buy shares of SpaceX for the first time. SpaceX is a rocket company in the United States. It started in 2002.
This was the biggest first day on the stock market in history.
The first price was 135 dollars. At the end of the day, one share cost 161 dollars. The price went up 19 percent.
The owner of the company is Elon Musk. He also runs Tesla, a car company. After this day, Musk became the first trillionaire in the world.
A trillion is a very big number. It is one thousand billion.
SpaceX sends rockets into space. It also has Starlink. Starlink gives internet from space to people on Earth.
Some people are excited. Other people ask a difficult question: is one company really worth so much money?

opts: How SpaceX builds rockets it can use again
How Elon Musk's car company makes money
How Starlink sends internet from space
SpaceX selling shares for the first time

opts: It went up from 135 to 161 dollars
It went down from 161 to 135 dollars
It stayed at 135 dollars
It went up from 75 to 135 dollars
q.why: 原文：“The first price was 135 dollars.”

q.q: What does Starlink do?
opts: It builds reusable rockets
It gives internet from space
It makes electric cars
It sells SpaceX shares
q.why: 原文：“Starlink gives internet from space to people on Earth.”

opts: pieces of a rocket that can be used again

opts: People have different opinions about the news
Everyone agrees SpaceX is worth the price

q.why: 線索：“On June 12, people could buy shares of SpaceX for the first time.”

q.q: Your cousin says: “The price went up on day one, so it will always go up.” What does the text suggest?
opts: True — when a price goes up on day one, it never comes down
True — every part of SpaceX already makes a lot of money
Not sure — some experts are careful because it lost a lot of money
Not true — the price actually fell on the very first day
q.why: 文中提到分析師持謹慎態度。

gt.zh: 六月十二日，人們第一次可以買 SpaceX 的股票。

gt.zh: 這是股市歷史上規模最大的上市首日。

gt.zh: 這天之後，馬斯克成為了全世界第一位兆萬富翁。

b.title: SpaceX Breaks the Record for the Largest IPO
text: On 12 June, shares in SpaceX were sold to the public for the first time, in what became the largest initial public offering, or IPO, ever completed. The company raised roughly 75 billion dollars — far more than the previous record of about 29 billion, set by the oil company Saudi Aramco in 2019.

The shares were priced at 135 dollars before trading began. By the close of the first day they had reached 161 dollars, a rise of 19 percent, and the company was valued at around two trillion dollars.
The result had a striking personal consequence. Because of the stakes he holds in both SpaceX and the carmaker Tesla, Elon Musk is now widely reported to be the world's first trillionaire.

SpaceX was founded in 2002 to build reusable rockets, but its satellite internet service, Starlink, is the part of the business that currently makes a profit. According to the company's own filing, SpaceX has lost more than 41 billion dollars in total since it was founded.

This gap has made some analysts cautious. They point out that the company's value is roughly 94 times its annual revenue, whereas established technology giants trade at far lower multiples. Supporters reply that investors are not buying today's earnings, but a share of what space and satellite technology may become.
gloss: （向主管機關提交的）申報文件

q.q: Which statement best summarises the text?
opts: SpaceX raised about 75 billion dollars from investors.
Elon Musk became the world's first trillionaire this year.
SpaceX set an IPO record, but its true value is debated.
Starlink is the part of SpaceX that makes a profit.

q.q: Which part of SpaceX is profitable at the moment?
opts: Its reusable rockets, built since 2002
Starlink, the satellite internet service
Its plans for trips to the Moon and Mars
Tesla, the carmaker that Musk also owns
q.why: 文中；Tesla 是另一家公司。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “cautious” is closest in meaning to ___.
opts: very excited and eager to buy
angry and upset about the price
completely against the company
careful and not fully convinced

q.q: Why do the analysts mention “94 times its annual revenue”?
opts: To suggest the price may be high compared with earnings
To show that the company makes huge profits every year
To compare SpaceX's record with Saudi Aramco's in 2019
To show how many shares were sold on the first day
q.why: 線索：“They point out that the company's value is roughly 94 times its annual revenue, whereas established technology giants trade at far lower multiples.”

q.q: How do supporters answer the analysts' concern?
opts: SpaceX already earns more than other technology giants.
Investors are buying what space technology may become.
The company has never lost money since it was founded.
The share price will soon fall to a more sensible level.
q.why: 原文：“Supporters reply that investors are not buying today's earnings, but a share of what space and satellite technology may become.”

q.q: Which fact from the text would a cautious investor point to MOST?
opts: SpaceX has lost over 41 billion dollars since it was founded

q.why: 長期虧損是謹慎的主要理由。

tr.en: The shares were priced at 135 dollars before trading began.
tr.zh: 在開始交易之前，股票的定價是 135 美元。

tr.zh: 根據公司自己提交的文件，SpaceX 自成立以來總共虧損了超過四百一十億美元。

tr.en: They point out that the company's value is roughly 94 times its annual revenue, whereas established technology giants trade at far lower multiples.
tr.zh: 他們指出，這家公司的市值大約是它年營收的 94 倍，而老牌科技巨頭的倍數則低得多。

c.title: Pricing the Future: What a Record IPO Actually Measures
text: When SpaceX shares began trading on 12 June, the numbers did what record-breaking numbers usually do: they crowded out the more interesting question. Some 75 billion dollars was raised, comfortably eclipsing the 29 billion that Saudi Aramco had secured in 2019; the stock closed its first session 19 percent above its offer price; and Elon Musk, by virtue of his holdings in SpaceX and Tesla, was declared the world's first trillionaire. What none of these figures establishes is whether the valuation is sound.

The case for caution is not difficult to assemble. A company founded in 2002 has, by its own account, accumulated losses exceeding 41 billion dollars, and only Starlink — the satellite internet arm — reliably generates profit. At roughly 94 times annual revenue, the valuation implies growth of an order that few firms in any sector have delivered. Compared with the multiples at which mature technology companies trade, the figure looks less like a measurement than an aspiration.

The counter-argument, however, is not merely wishful. Investors in genuinely novel industries have rarely been pricing current earnings; they are pricing optionality — the possibility that a dominant launch provider becomes the infrastructure on which an entire orbital economy is eventually built. Whether that argument is prescient or self-serving cannot be settled by the share price on any given afternoon.

What the debut does demonstrate, unambiguously, is appetite. Whatever their private reservations, enough investors were willing to commit capital at that price to make the offering the largest ever completed. Markets, in this sense, are not verdicts on the future; they are collections of bets on it. The distinction is easy to lose when the headline number is large enough — and this one was very large indeed.
gloss: 選擇權價值；未來可能性

q.q: What is the writer's central claim?
opts: SpaceX is clearly overvalued, as its long history of losses proves.
SpaceX is clearly worth two trillion dollars, as the market showed.

q.q: How does the writer treat the two sides of the debate?
opts: Strongly supports the analysts' warnings about losses

q.q: In paragraph 2, “less like a measurement than an aspiration” implies that the valuation ___.
opts: reflects hope about the future more than present facts

is much lower than most analysts had expected

q.q: What does the writer mean by “Markets… are not verdicts on the future; they are collections of bets on it”?
opts: Markets can predict the future accurately if enough people buy.
Investors are simply gamblers who usually end up losing money.
A high price shows what investors will risk, not what is proven.

q.why: 線索：“Whatever their private reservations, enough investors were willing to commit capital at that price to make the offering the largest ever completed.”

q.q: Which best describes the structure of the text?
opts: History of the company → records → final judgement
Problem → proposed solution → result for investors
Records → caution → counter-argument → what it does prove

q.q: Which question would best help decide whether the valuation is justified?
opts: How many people around the world watched the IPO happen live?
Will Starlink and future services earn enough to match the price?
How much exactly did the shares rise by the end of day one?

q.why: 估值是否合理取決於未來獲利。

Would you invest in a company that loses money now but might be important in the future?

src: The New York Times · The Washington Post · BBC Sport

a.title: Spain and Argentina in the Final
text: Spain will play Argentina on Sunday, July 19. It is the World Cup final. The game is at a big stadium near New York City.
This World Cup is very special. Three countries are the hosts: the United States, Mexico, and Canada. Forty-eight teams played 104 games. The first game was on June 11.
Argentina won the World Cup in 2022. Lionel Messi is their captain. Spain won the World Cup only one time, in 2010. Lamine Yamal is their young star.
In the semi-finals, Spain beat France 2–0. Argentina beat England. Now only two teams are left.
The three host countries all lost early in the games. Their fans were very sad.
Millions of people around the world will watch the final.

The World Cup final on Sunday

b.title: Spain Meet Argentina in a Record-Breaking Final
text: On Sunday, 19 July, Spain will face Argentina in the final of the 2026 World Cup at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. It will be the last match of a tournament that has broken several records.

This was the first World Cup to be hosted by three countries — the United States, Mexico and Canada — and the first to include 48 teams instead of 32. In total, 104 matches were played across 16 stadiums.

Argentina are the defending champions, having won the trophy in 2022. In the semi-final in Atlanta, they were behind against England before Lionel Messi inspired a late comeback. Messi has also become the first player to reach ten assists in World Cup matches since such records began in 1966.

Spain, who have won the tournament only once, reached their first final in sixteen years by defeating France 2–0 in Dallas. Their teenage forward Lamine Yamal has been one of the stars of the competition.
For the host nations, however, the tournament ended in disappointment. All three were knocked out in the round of 16, so no home team reached the quarter-finals.
Whichever team lifts the trophy on Sunday, the 2026 World Cup will be remembered as the largest in the competition's history.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the text?
opts: Spain reached their first final in sixteen years.
The final ends a tournament that set new records.
Messi inspired a late comeback against England.

opts: It had 32 teams and one host country.
It had 104 teams.

It was the first held in the United States.
q.why: 原文：“This was the first World Cup to be hosted by three countries — the United States, Mexico and Canada — and the first to include 48 teams instead of 32.”

q.q: In paragraph 5, “knocked out” is closest in meaning to ___.
opts: injured badly during a match
winning a game very easily

q.why: 線索：“For the host nations, however, the tournament ended in disappointment.”

q.q: What record has Messi set at this World Cup?

q.why: 原文：“Messi has also become the first player to reach ten assists in World Cup matches since such records began in 1966.”

q.q: A TV reporter says: “This was the most successful World Cup for the host nations.” Based on the text, is this accurate?
opts: Yes — it was the biggest World Cup ever played
Yes — the final is being played in New Jersey
No — the hosts were not allowed to play at all
No — all three hosts went out in the round of 16

tr.en: It will be the last match of a tournament that has broken several records.
tr.zh: 這將是一場打破多項紀錄的賽事的最後一場比賽。

tr.zh: 在亞特蘭大的準決賽中，他們原本落後英格蘭，後來梅西帶領球隊在比賽尾聲逆轉。

tr.en: Spain, who have won the tournament only once, reached their first final in sixteen years by defeating France 2–0 in Dallas.
tr.zh: 只拿過一次冠軍的西班牙，在達拉斯以二比零擊敗法國，十六年來第一次打進決賽。

c.title: A Tournament of Records — and of Absences
text: When Spain and Argentina walk out at MetLife Stadium on Sunday evening, they will bring to a close a World Cup defined as much by its scale as by its football. Expanded from 32 teams to 48 and shared, for the first time, among three host nations, the 2026 tournament stretched across nearly six weeks and 104 matches — a logistical undertaking that would have been almost unthinkable a generation ago.

The final itself offers a study in contrasts. Argentina arrive as holders, carried once again by Lionel Messi, whose late intervention against England in Atlanta rescued a semi-final that had appeared to be slipping away. That he has now supplied more assists than any player since such records were first kept in 1966 says as much about longevity as it does about genius. Spain, by contrast, are chasing a second star: their only previous triumph came in 2010, and much of their attacking threat now runs through a forward who was barely three years old when that victory was won.

Yet for all the records, this tournament may equally be remembered for who was absent from its closing stages. All three hosts — the United States, Mexico and Canada — exited in the round of 16, denying organisers precisely the home narrative on which such events are so often built. Whether an expanded format ultimately dilutes the competition or genuinely broadens its reach remains a matter of legitimate debate; what is beyond dispute is that the 2026 edition has been the largest the sport has ever staged.
Sunday, in the end, will settle only one question: whether Argentina retain what they won in Qatar, or whether Spain add a second title to a wait that has now lasted sixteen years.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: The 48-team format was a clear success, as the records show.
The 48-team format failed because the hosts went out early.
Messi's assist record is the main story of the tournament.
Its record scale sits alongside all three hosts' early exit.

q.q: How would you describe the writer's attitude to the 48-team format?
opts: Deliberately balanced and non-committal
Strongly in favour of the bigger format
Strongly against adding more teams

q.q: In paragraph 3, “denying organisers precisely the home narrative” suggests that the hosts' exit ___.
opts: forced organisers to change the rules of the tournament
stopped organisers telling a story they had counted on
gave organisers a better story than the one they planned
was secretly planned by organisers to help other teams

Messi now plays only a short time in each match he starts.
His record partly reflects how long he has played at the top.
Several other players have actually made more assists.
q.why: 線索：“That he has now supplied more assists than any player since such records were first kept in 1966 says as much about longevity as it does about genius.”

q.q: What is the function of the word “Yet” at the start of paragraph 3?
opts: To shift to a contrasting, less celebratory point
To add more records that the tournament broke
To introduce the two teams playing in the final
To bring the article to a positive conclusion

q.q: To judge whether the 48-team format was a success, which evidence would be MOST useful?
opts: The number of stadiums used across the three hosts
Messi's ten assists since records began in 1966
Attendance and how competitive the extra games were
The stadium and city chosen to host the final
q.why: 評估賽制需要與舊賽制比較的多項證據。
